# Summary

"The Strange Case of Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde" is a classic novella by Robert Louis Stevenson, available through Project Gutenberg as a free eBook (released June 27, 2008; most recently updated May 12, 2026). The work is in English and explores the dual nature of its protagonist through nine chapters, beginning with "Story of the Door" and progressing through various mysterious incidents involving Mr. Hyde, the murder of Carew, and letters involving Dr. Lanyon, culminating in Dr. Jekyll's full confession. The eBook can be freely copied and distributed under Project Gutenberg License terms, with additional formats available at www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/43.

# Summary

Mr. Utterson, a reserved but tolerant lawyer, regularly takes Sunday walks with his distant kinsman Richard Enfield through London. During one such walk, Enfield points out a neglected, sinister door on a by-street and recounts a disturbing incident: he once witnessed a small man named Hyde callously trample a young girl, then calmly walk away. When confronted by an angry mob and threatened with exposure, Hyde agreed to pay compensation and led them to the mysterious door, where he produced a large cheque signed by a well-known, respectable man—suggesting blackmail. Though Enfield refuses to ask questions about the door's occupants, Utterson's reaction reveals he already knows the identity of the cheque's drawer. Both men agree never to discuss the matter again, leaving the nature of Hyde's connection to the door and the respectable man unexplained.

# Summary

Mr. Utterson, a lawyer, becomes deeply disturbed after reviewing Dr. Jekyll's will, which bequeaths all of Jekyll's possessions to the mysterious Edward Hyde, even granting Hyde control should Jekyll disappear for three months. Seeking information, Utterson visits his old friend Dr. Lanyon, who reveals he has not seen Jekyll in over ten years due to Jekyll's increasingly "fanciful" and unscientific pursuits. After a sleepless night plagued by nightmarish visions of Hyde as a malevolent figure trampling a child, Utterson begins nightly vigils outside Jekyll's house, hoping to catch a glimpse of Hyde. Finally encountering the small, pale, and deeply unsettling Mr. Hyde entering the house with a key, Utterson obtains his address in Soho and meets him face-to-face. Though unable to articulate precisely why, Utterson finds Hyde repulsive and inhuman—sensing a profound evil emanating from him. After questioning Dr. Jekyll's butler Poole, Utterson learns that Hyde has a key to the laboratory and possesses Jekyll's complete trust

# Summary

During a dinner at Dr. Jekyll's home, Mr. Utterson remains behind to speak privately with the doctor about his will, which leaves his estate to the mysterious young man Mr. Hyde. When Utterson expresses his disapproval and mentions learning disturbing things about Hyde, Jekyll becomes visibly distressed and evasive, insisting the matter cannot be discussed or remedied through conversation. Though Utterson offers his help and confidentiality, Jekyll refuses to explain his situation, claiming he can rid himself of Hyde whenever he chooses. He instead asks Utterson to promise that if something happens to him, he will ensure Hyde receives fair treatment and his rightful inheritance—a request Utterson reluctantly agrees to, though he makes clear his personal dislike of the young man.

# Summary

In October, London is shocked by the brutal murder of the prominent Sir Danvers Carew, witnessed by a maid who observes a small, wicked-looking man named Mr. Hyde violently attack an elderly gentleman with a cane in a moonlit lane. The murder weapon—a broken stick—is identified by lawyer Mr. Utterson as one he had given to Henry Jekyll years before. The envelope found on the victim is addressed to Utterson, arousing his suspicion. When Utterson and Inspector Newcomen visit Hyde's modest Soho residence, they discover ransacked rooms, burned papers, and the other half of the murder stick, along with evidence of substantial funds in Hyde's bank account. Although the inspector believes he can easily apprehend Hyde, the fugitive proves difficult to locate, having few acquaintances and never being photographed; witnesses can only agree that he bears an inexplicable sense of deformity.

# Summary

Late afternoon, Mr. Utterson visits Dr. Jekyll at his laboratory and finds him looking deathly ill. After learning that news of a murder (of Sir Danvers Carew, Utterson's client) has spread, Utterson asks if Jekyll has hidden the culprit, Edward Hyde. Jekyll swears he will never see Hyde again and reveals he has received a letter from Hyde claiming he has means of escape and will trouble Jekyll no further. Though Utterson finds the letter reassuring, he grows suspicious when he discovers no messenger delivered it—it must have come through the laboratory door. Later, Utterson shows the letter to his head clerk, Mr. Guest, a handwriting expert, ostensibly for counsel. Guest notices the handwriting is nearly identical to Jekyll's own, though differently sloped. Deeply disturbed by this revelation, Utterson locks the letter away, realizing that Jekyll may have forged it for the murderer.

# Summary

Following Sir Danvers Carew's murder and Mr. Hyde's mysterious disappearance, Dr. Jekyll initially appears to recover and resume a normal social life with renewed religiosity and charity. However, when lawyer Utterson visits Dr. Lanyon on January 15th, he finds him gravely ill and visibly deteriorated, apparently dying from psychological terror rather than physical ailment. Lanyon cryptically refuses to discuss Jekyll, declaring him "dead" and begging Utterson to avoid the topic. Jekyll writes to Utterson explaining he must live in complete seclusion due to an unnamed punishment and danger he has brought upon himself. Lanyon dies within a fortnight, leaving Utterson a sealed envelope marked to be opened only after Jekyll's death or disappearance—a mysterious echo of Jekyll's original will. Intrigued but bound by professional honor, Utterson safeguards the envelope while growing increasingly uncomfortable with Jekyll's isolation and reclusiveness, eventually distancing himself from his old friend.

# Summary

During a Sunday walk through a familiar by-street, Mr. Utterson and his cousin Mr. Enfield encounter Dr. Jekyll at a window of his residence. Utterson, concerned about Jekyll's wellbeing, attempts to encourage him to take a walk with them, but Jekyll declines, claiming he cannot leave. When Jekyll agrees to speak with them from the window instead, his expression suddenly transforms into one of absolute terror and despair before he abruptly closes the window and disappears. Deeply shaken and pale, the two men leave the court in stunned silence, unable to speak until reaching a busier street, where they exchange horrified glances and Utterson utters a prayer for forgiveness.

# Combined Summary

One evening, butler Poole urgently visits lawyer Utterson with grave concerns about Dr. Jekyll, who has locked himself in his cabinet for a week. Upon investigating Jekyll's residence with Poole, Utterson discovers the servants are terrified and learns that Poole witnessed a masked, dwarf-like figure resembling Mr. Hyde retrieving chemicals. After breaking down the cabinet door, they find Edward Hyde's dead body—an apparent suicide by poison—but Jekyll's body is nowhere to be found. On Jekyll's desk, they discover a dated note indicating Jekyll is alive but has disappeared and anticipates an imminent end. The note instructs Utterson to read narratives from both Lanyon and Jekyll himself, which Poole provides in sealed packets. Utterson decides to keep the matter quiet to protect Jekyll's reputation and plans to examine these documents before midnight, after which he intends to contact the police.

# Summary

Dr. Lanyon receives an urgent, cryptic letter from his colleague Dr. Jekyll requesting that he retrieve a drawer containing powders, a blood-red phial, and a notebook from Jekyll's locked cabinet and deliver it to a mysterious messenger at midnight. Though bewildered and suspecting Jekyll's insanity, Lanyon complies. When the small, oddly-dressed stranger arrives at midnight, he urgently demands the drawer and prepares a mixture from its contents. After drinking the concoction, the man undergoes a horrifying transformation before Lanyon's eyes, revealing himself to be Dr. Jekyll. Lanyon is profoundly traumatized by Jekyll's subsequent confession—later revealed to involve the murderer Hyde—which shatters his understanding of reality and leaves him physically and mentally broken, unable to reconcile what he witnessed with rational belief.

# Combined Summary

Dr. Jekyll, born into wealth and virtue, develops a scientific potion that physically separates his dual nature into two distinct entities: his respectable self and Edward Hyde, a purely malevolent alter ego. Initially, Jekyll uses this ability to indulge his base desires while maintaining his reputation, but gradually loses control as Hyde grows stronger and more dominant. After committing an unprovoked murder as Hyde, Jekyll briefly reforms through charitable work but succumbs to temptation once more. Trapped as the wanted murderer after an involuntary transformation in Regent's Park, Hyde desperately retrieves the antidote drug through Dr. Lanyon. However, the situation deteriorates catastrophically as the drug's effectiveness wanes, transformations occur with increasing frequency and less warning, and Hyde grows increasingly malevolent and dominant. Jekyll weakens physically and mentally while Hyde revels in acts of spite, revealing the inescapable consequences of attempting to separate human nature's dual aspects.

During one such walk, Enfield points out a neglected, sinister door on a by-street and recounts a disturbing incident: he once witnessed a small man named Hyde callously trample a young girl, then calmly walk away. When confronted by an angry mob and threatened with exposure, Hyde agreed to pay compensation and led them to the mysterious door, where he produced a large cheque signed by a well-known, respectable man—a revelation suggesting blackmail that unsettles both men. Though Enfield refuses to ask questions about the door's occupants, Utterson's reaction reveals he already knows the identity of the cheque's drawer, and both men agree never to discuss the matter again.

This initial unease proves prophetic when Utterson reviews Dr. Jekyll's will, which bequeaths all of Jekyll's possessions to the mysterious Edward Hyde and grants Hyde control should Jekyll disappear for three months. Seeking context, Utterson visits his old friend Dr. Lanyon, who reveals he has not seen Jekyll in over ten years due to Jekyll's increasingly "fanciful" and unscientific pursuits. Plagued by nightmarish visions of Hyde as a malevolent figure trampling a child, Utterson begins nightly vigils outside Jekyll's house, eventually encountering the small, pale, and deeply unsettling Mr. Hyde entering with a key. Meeting Hyde face-to-face, Utterson finds him repulsive and inhuman, sensing a profound evil emanating from him, and discovers that Hyde possesses a key to Jekyll's laboratory and enjoys his complete trust.

These initial concerns prove warranted as Jekyll's true situation emerges in shocking detail. Jekyll was born into wealth and virtue but developed a scientific potion that physically separates his dual nature into two distinct entities: his respectable self and Edward Hyde, a purely malevolent alter ego. Initially using this ability to indulge base desires while maintaining his reputation, Jekyll's control gradually deteriorates as Hyde grows stronger and increasingly dominant. The situation turns catastrophic when London is shocked by the brutal murder of prominent Sir Danvers Carew, witnessed by a maid observing Hyde violently attacking the elderly gentleman with a cane—a murder weapon identified as one Utterson had given Jekyll years before, arousing immediate suspicion and linking Jekyll directly to the crime.

When Utterson and Inspector Newcomen investigate Hyde's modest Soho residence, they discover ransacked rooms, burned papers, and evidence of substantial funds, yet Hyde remains difficult to locate. During a dinner at Jekyll's home, Utterson expresses his disapproval of the will, and Jekyll becomes visibly distressed and evasive, refusing to discuss or remedy the matter. Despite Utterson's offers of help, Jekyll insists he can rid himself of Hyde whenever he chooses, but then asks Utterson to promise that if something happens to him, Hyde will receive fair treatment and his rightful inheritance—a reluctant agreement Utterson makes.

Following the Carew murder, Jekyll's deterioration accelerates dramatically. When Utterson visits him at his laboratory, he finds Jekyll looking deathly ill and learns that news of the crime has deeply affected him. Jekyll swears he will never see Hyde again and reveals he has received a letter from Hyde claiming means of escape, yet Utterson's suspicion deepens when he discovers no messenger delivered it—it must have arrived through the laboratory door itself. His head clerk Mr. Guest, a handwriting expert, analyzes the letter with disturbing results: the handwriting is nearly identical to Jekyll's own though differently sloped, forcing Utterson to confront the possibility that Jekyll himself forged the letter, suggesting sinister collusion.

Utterson's suspicions are further confirmed when he visits Dr. Lanyon and finds him gravely ill, apparently dying from psychological terror rather than physical ailment. Lanyon cryptically refuses to discuss Jekyll, declaring him "dead" and begging Utterson to avoid the topic. His deterioration stems from a horrifying midnight encounter in which he witnessed the small, oddly-dressed stranger drink a concoction and undergo a grotesque transformation, revealing himself to be Dr. Jekyll—a revelation that shatters Lanyon's understanding of reality and leads to his death within a fortnight.

Jekyll's grip on his circumstances finally collapses as his isolation deepens into complete reclusiveness. When Utterson encounters him during a Sunday walk, Jekyll's expression transforms into absolute terror before he abruptly closes the window and disappears. As Jekyll locks himself away entirely, butler Poole urgently visits Utterson with grave concerns. Upon investigating, they discover a masked, dwarf-like figure and Edward Hyde's dead body, apparently a suicide by poison, with Jekyll's body nowhere to be found. A dated note indicates Jekyll is alive but has disappeared, instructing Utterson to read sealed narratives before midnight—revealing the inescapable consequences of attempting to separate human nature's dual aspects.
